newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan scandal is school for "Big Bang" ethics.
newsitem.headline: Japan scandal is school for "Big Bang" ethics.

text.p: A high-profile scandal at two of Japan's top financial institutions is proving a golden opportunity to teach a timely lesson in corporate ethics as Tokyo gears up for its "Big Bang" financial deregulation.

Speculation persists that the scandal at giant Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB) will ensnare other financial firms, though many experts predict it could end with authorities making a harsh example of the two big players.
Either way, those who expect business as usual after loud expressions of outrage and regret over corporate misdeeds might be well-advised to check their scepticism at the door.

"I think it is not a pose, I think they are sending a very strong message that transparency and accountability are what the 'Big Bang' is really about," said one foreign analyst. "It's not just form, it's also content."

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has staked much of his still-shaky reputation as a reformer on the success of a plan to tear down walls between financial sectors and subject the nation's once-protected banks, brokers and insurers to real competition.

That success hinges not only on scrapping government regulations but on altering a business mind-set which obscures accountability, and the scandal is turning into a high-profile object lesson to those from the old school of management.
Prosecutors last week arrested four DKB officials on suspicion of illegally extending uncollateralised loans to Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" corporate racketeer at the heart of the scandal.

Prosecutors have indicted Nomura itself for violating the securities law by illegally compensating a firm run by Koike's younger brother, as well as two former Nomura directors for violating both securities law and the Commercial Code.

Former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki has also been arrested and prosecutors have reportedly questioned former chairman Setsuya Tabuchi and former president Yoshihisa Tabuchi in connection with the scandal.

That the two Tabuchis (no relation), are again under fire might at first blush suggest that little has changed since the two resigned their posts in 1991 over scandals involving improper client compensation and business ties with gangsters.
The two men retained influence over Nomura management and returned to its board in 1995, only to be forced to step down again in a sweeping management shake-up last month.
But financial experts say authorities' attitude has altered since the 1991 scandals, which ironically forced Hashimoto to resign as finance minister.
Those affairs entangled most of the nation's brokerages and many top banks but ended without arrests of senior executives.
"I think they are more eager to press criminal sanctions against Nomura and DKB," said an international lawyer. "It's certainly promising that they are arresting so many people."

Still, doubts persist over whether authorities are prepared to follow the scandal trail if, as many believe, it leads to the boardrooms of other financial institutions or down the political corridors of power.

"Koike was a high-living type and the alleged payments by Nomura would barely pay his cigar and bar bills," the lawyer said. "Will they go after all the other companies that are doing the same thing? They should, but they may not."

A spokesman for the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission on Friday declined comment on Japanese media reports that the securities watchdog was investigating the other three of Japan's Big Four brokerages in connection with the scandal.
Spokesmen for Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd and Daiwa Securities Co Ltd also declined comment.
Some in the financial industry are betting that authorities will come down hard on Nomura and DKB, and stop there.
"Are they picking on the strong because they can take it? Yes, they are. It's always the industry leader that sets the example," the foreign analyst said.
The message may, in fact, finally be getting through.
"Other banks are scurrying to put a lid on their links with sokaiya," one Japanese banker said.
But arrests and administrative punishment, however harsh, may still not be enough to alter the mentality that winks at ties with the underworld and other misdeeds, some experts said.

"The other question is the willingness of the system and the judges to impose criminal sentences," the lawyer said. "It's not enough to take pictures of people in cars riding to the police station. At the end of the process, people really have to go to jail," he said.
